claim: 2800 IU/day Vitamin D3 for 12 weeks significantly reduced handgrip strength by 9% and knee flexion strength by 13% in postmenopausal women with vitamin D insufficiency — a small unfavorable effect on muscle strength.
stance_target: high-dose D3 supplementation universally benefits muscle function
scope_conditions: RCT, n=81 postmenopausal women, 25(OH)D <50 nmol/L, elevated PTH, 12 weeks, 56°N latitude, wintertime
quoted_support: Compared with placebo, vitamin D3 significantly reduced maximal handgrip strength by 9% (−15 to −3%; p<0.01) and knee flexion strength by 13% (−24 to −2%; p=0.02) and increased the time spent on performing the Timed Up and Go test by 4.4%; (0.1–8.6%; p<0.05).

claim: 2800 IU/day D3 supplementation raised 25(OH)D by 230% and reduced PTH by 17% in vitamin D-insufficient women, but this normalization did not translate into muscle health benefits.
stance_target: correcting vitamin D insufficiency improves multiple health outcomes
scope_conditions: RCT, postmenopausal women with D insufficiency and elevated PTH, 12 weeks
quoted_support: Vitamin D3 supplementation increased levels of 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D by 230% (95% CI 189 to 272)%, p<0.001 and 58% (190 to 271%), p<0.001, respectively, and reduced PTH by 17% (−23 to −11%), p<0.001.

claim: Authors call for caution with 'relatively high daily doses' of D3 (2800 IU/day) in treating vitamin D insufficiency; 2000 IU/day remains well below the threshold showing adverse muscle effects in this trial.
stance_target: 2000 IU daily is a conservative safe dose that avoids adverse muscle effects seen at 2800 IU
scope_conditions: Authors' recommendation based on their 2800 IU trial findings; applies to postmenopausal women with D insufficiency
quoted_support: Our data call for caution on use of relatively high daily doses of vitamin D3 in the treatment of vitamin D insufficiency.
numbers: 2000 IU Briyo dose = below problematic threshold
